answer.why_different: The generated document uses shorter response descriptions and replaces the official generic `default` error response with explicit `4XX` and `5XX` response ranges. This is primarily a difference in response values and response-key structure, rather than an address-level difference.
answer.spec_3gpp: The 3GPP evidence identifies the PUT response body as a `Resource` and requires response status-code handling; it also identifies an `ErrorResponse` for error responses. The generated descriptions omit some of the success-case conditions and response semantics carried by the official descriptions. [S6] [S7]
answer.openapi: OpenAPI 3.0 requires response descriptions and permits both a `default` response for otherwise undeclared codes and uppercase wildcard response ranges such as `4XX` and `5XX`. Therefore, the explicit ranges are structurally valid, but replacing `default` can reduce coverage of response codes not included in those ranges. [O3] [O5] [O6] [O10]
answer.clearer_why: The official success descriptions explain when each status code is returned and whether a representation is present, while the generated descriptions are substantially less informative. The explicit error ranges are recognizable, but they do not compensate for the lost success-case detail.

differences.reason: The generated description is a shorter summary, but it omits the official conditions distinguishing replacement, update, and representation identity, as well as the response-representation detail. This loses information about the 200 response; the PUT operation returns a `Resource` in the response body. [S6]

`Created` is accurate but omits the official statement that this status is returned when the resource is created and that the created representation is returned in the response body. The response body is a documented PUT output in the 3GPP mapping. [S6] [S16]

`No Content` conveys the basic status meaning but omits the important restriction that 204 may be used only when the replacement is identical to the request representation. This loses behaviorally relevant information from the official response description. [S7]

OpenAPI permits omitting `default`, because it is optional, but `default` is specifically intended to cover response codes not declared individually. The evidence does not establish whether the PUT operation can return errors outside the generated `4XX` and `5XX` ranges. [O3] [O6]

An uppercase `4XX` response range is an allowed OpenAPI 3.0 response key and explicitly documents client-error responses. The 3GPP evidence supports an error response for the PUT operation, although it does not require this particular range notation. [S7] [O5]

An uppercase `5XX` response range is an allowed OpenAPI 3.0 response key and explicitly documents server-error responses. The 3GPP evidence supports an error response for the PUT operation, although it does not require this particular range notation. [S7] [O5]

#### Responses Object  
A container for the expected responses of an operation.
The container maps a HTTP response code to the expected response.  
The documentation is not necessarily expected to cover all possible HTTP response codes because they may not be known in advance.
However, documentation is expected to cover a successful operation response and any known errors.  
The `default` MAY be used as a default response object for all HTTP codes
that are not covered individually by the specification.  
The `Responses Object` MUST contain at least one response code, and it
SHOULD be the response for a successful operation call.

##### Support for x-www-form-urlencoded Request Bodies  
To submit content using form url encoding via [RFC1866](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc1866), the following
definition may be used:  
```yaml
requestBody:
content:
application/x-www-form-urlencoded:
schema:
type: object
properties:
id:
type: string
format: uuid
address:
# complex types are stringified to support RFC 1866
type: object
properties: {}
```  
In this example, the contents in the `requestBody` MUST be stringified per [RFC1866](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc1866/) when passed to the server.  In addition, the `address` field complex object will be stringified.  
When passing complex objects in the `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content type, the default serialization strategy of such properties is described in the [`Encoding Object`](#encoding-object)'s [`style`](#encodingStyle) property as `form`.

evidence.text: Describes a single response from an API Operation, including design-time, static `links` to operations based on the response. ##### Fixed Fields Field Name | Type | Description ---|:---:|--- description | `string` | **REQUIRED**. A short description of the response. [CommonMark syntax](http://spec.commonmark.org/) MAY be used for rich text representation. headers | Map[`string`, [Header Object](#header-object) \| [Reference Object](#reference-object)] | Maps a header name to its definition. [RFC7230](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7230#page-22) states header names are case insensitive. If a response header is defined with the name `"Content-Type"`, it SHALL be ignored.
